title: Express and Node: middleware order, request shape, and what reaches the filesystem

threat_model.actor: Any caller who can send an HTTP request to the process, including one who addresses a route the user interface never links to and one who chooses the shape, not just the value, of every request field
threat_model.asset: The handlers behind the middleware stack, the objects the application builds from request data, the files under any served root, and the memory the process allocates per request
threat_model.trust_boundary: The ordered chain of `app.use` and route registrations: everything registered before a guard runs without it, and everything the guard does not match is reached directly
threat_model.failure_mode: A guard is present and looks global, but the route reached is registered earlier in the stack, is mounted on a different router, or matches a pattern the guard's path does not, so the handler executes without it
threat_model.impact: A handler runs for a caller the application intended to reject, an object is built with properties the caller chose, a path resolves outside the intended root, or an error response carries the stack and internal state back to the caller

required_evidence: A Node.js entry point that constructs an application with `express()` or mounts `express.Router()` instances, or a `package.json` declaring `express` as a dependency
At least one request-handling function that reads `req.body`, `req.params`, `req.query`, or `req.headers` and uses the value to select data, build an object, or resolve a path

signals: A route handler registered above the `app.use(authenticate)` line, so the stack reaches it before the guard exists
`router.use(guard)` in one router while a second router mounted on an overlapping path has no equivalent
A guard mounted on a path prefix — `app.use('/api', guard)` — while handlers are also registered at a sibling prefix that the mount does not cover
An early `next()` or a conditional `return next()` inside a guard that continues the chain on the failure branch as well as the success branch
Error-handling middleware declared with fewer than four parameters, so Express treats it as ordinary middleware and it never receives errors

versions: 4.x defaults the `query parser` setting to `extended`, which parses `a[b]=c` into a nested object using qs
5.x defaults the `query parser` setting to `simple`, which uses the Node `querystring` module and keeps `a[b]` as a literal key
either version can be reconfigured with `app.set('query parser', ...)`, so the setting decides the behaviour and the version only decides the default
signals: Code that assumes `req.query.x` is a string — calling a string method on it, comparing it, or passing it into a query builder — while the configured parser can produce an object or an array
A repeated query parameter treated as a single value, where the two parsers disagree about whether the result is an array or the last value
`req.params` used as an identifier in a data lookup with no check that the caller may reach that object
An Express 5 upgrade in which route patterns were rewritten for the new path syntax, so a guard's path may no longer match the routes it used to cover
A recursive merge or deep-assign helper applied to `req.body`, where a key named `__proto__` or `constructor` is copied rather than skipped
Whole-body assignment into a model or update document, so any property the caller sends becomes a property the application persists
A configuration or options object built by merging caller-supplied JSON into a shared default object rather than into a fresh one
Object keys used to index into a lookup table without checking that the key is an own property of that table
`express.json`, `express.urlencoded`, `express.text`, or `express.raw` mounted with an explicitly raised `limit`, or a third-party parser mounted with none
A body parser mounted globally so it runs for routes that never read a body, including unauthenticated ones
An endpoint that accepts an array and performs one unit of work per element, with no cap on the element count
A file-upload middleware whose size and count limits are not set, or are set only in one of several mount points
An error handler that serialises the error object, `err.stack`, or `err.message` into the response body
Reliance on the framework's default error handler, whose response detail depends on `NODE_ENV`, in a deployment where `NODE_ENV` is not demonstrably set to `production`
`res.sendFile` or `res.download` called with a path built from request data and no `root` option
A path assembled with string concatenation or `path.join` from a request value and then opened directly, bypassing the containment `express.static` performs for its own root
`app.set('trust proxy', true)` or an equivalent that trusts every hop, making `req.ip` and the forwarded headers caller-controlled

boundary.subject: the caller as established by whichever middleware actually ran before the matched handler
boundary.object: the handler body, the objects it constructs from request data, and the files and memory it reaches
boundary.invariant: Every route that needs a guard is registered after that guard on a path the guard matches, and every value the handler takes from the request is constrained in both value and shape before it is used

examples: Handler registered before the authentication middleware
Handler on a router whose mount path the guard does not cover
Recursive merge of `req.body` into an options object
Whole-body assignment into a persisted model or update document
Query keyed on `req.params.id` with no ownership predicate
Filter object built from `req.query` whose value the parser turned into an object
`res.sendFile` with a request-derived path and no `root`
Path joined from a request value and opened directly
Stack trace serialised into the response body
Database driver error returned verbatim to the caller
Body parser with a raised or absent size limit
One unit of work per element of a caller-sized array

signals: Read the application file top to bottom as the stack it is, and for each route ask which middleware had already been registered when that route was added
For each request field the handler reads, ask what happens if the caller sends an array or an object instead of a string, and what happens if the key is `__proto__`
Ask what the caller learns from the error path, not just from the success path
Build the ordered list of every `app.use`, `app.METHOD`, `router.use`, and `router.METHOD` registration, including those inside imported route modules, and mark where each guard begins to apply
List every router mount point and check whether each one carries the same guard, since a second router is the usual place the guard is missing
Find every deep merge, spread, or assignment whose source is request-derived, and record whether `__proto__` and `constructor` are excluded
Record the configured `query parser` setting and the Express major version, then find every place the handler assumes a string
Find every filesystem call whose path derives from a request value and record whether containment is asserted after resolution
Find every error handler, count its parameters, and record what of the error object reaches the response
State which routes are intended to be public and compare that list with the routes the guard actually covers, rather than with the routes the developer believes it covers
State the expected type of every request field the handler uses and check that a validator enforces the type before use
Decide whether request size and element counts are bounded at the parser, at the route, or nowhere
Establish which directories the process can read under any served root, and whether anything sensitive is reachable from there
Establish whether `NODE_ENV` is set to `production` in the deployment being reasoned about, since the default error handler's response detail depends on it
Against a local instance, request each route with no credentials and record which return a handler response rather than a rejection
Send the same parameter as a string, as a repeated parameter, and in bracket notation, and record what `req.query` becomes under the configured parser
Send a body containing a `__proto__` key and afterwards read a property on a plain object created by the process, recording whether it changed
Trigger an error path and record exactly what the response body contains

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and run a local instance with synthetic data and the same middleware registration order as the deployment
Enumerate routes from the application's own router stack rather than from documentation, so routes nothing links to are included
Request each route with no credentials and with a second synthetic account's credentials, recording the status and body for each
Send each request field in string, repeated, and bracket-notation form, and log the resulting `req.query` and `req.body` values to observe the shape the parser produced

Send one request whose body contains a `__proto__` key, then read a property on a freshly created plain object in the same process and record whether it was affected; restart the process afterwards so no polluted state carries into later steps
Request a served path that resolves above the intended root and record whether the response is a refusal or file content, without reading any file outside the authorized test tree
Trigger a handler error and record the response body verbatim, together with the `NODE_ENV` value the process was started with
Keep body-size probes small enough to observe the limit boundary without exhausting the host, and stop at the first refusal

false_positive_filters: The route is registered after the guard and on a path the guard's mount covers; ordering, not the presence of the guard, is the question, so read the registration sequence before concluding either way
A second guard inside the handler or inside the service it calls re-establishes the caller, so the middleware gap has no consequence for that route
The route is intentionally public — health, static asset, webhook with its own signature verification — and its own verification is present and checked before any effect
The merge helper in use documents and implements `__proto__` and `constructor` skipping, or the target is created with a null prototype, so copying the key changes nothing reachable
The body is validated against a schema that rejects unknown keys and enforces types before any object is built from it, so shape confusion cannot occur downstream
The configured `query parser` is `simple`, so bracket notation stays a literal key and the object-shaped value the reviewer imagined is not producible from the query string
The path is passed to `res.sendFile` with a `root` option, or to `express.static`, both of which resolve and refuse to leave that root, so concatenation appearance is not escape
Containment is asserted after resolution — the resolved path is compared against the resolved root as a whole path component — so an encoded or traversing name cannot escape
The error handler returns a fixed message and an identifier, logging the detail server-side, so the stack the reviewer saw in the log never reaches the caller
Body size and element counts are bounded at the parser mount or by a validator, so the unbounded appearance in the handler is already constrained upstream
`trust proxy` is set to a specific hop count or a named proxy rather than to a blanket true, so forwarded headers are only honoured from the infrastructure that sets them

required_evidence: The ordered registration sequence showing the route and the guard, with the line numbers or module import order that establishes which came first
A recorded request and response showing the handler reached without the credentials the guard requires, alongside the same request with them
For a shape or pollution claim, the observed value of the parsed field and, for pollution, an observation on a separate object showing the prototype changed
For a path claim, the resolved absolute path and the intended root, showing the resolved path outside it
For a leakage claim, the response body as returned to the caller, together with the `NODE_ENV` the process ran under
refutation_tests: Re-read the application entry point and every imported route module in import order before asserting a guard is missing, since registration order is the control and it is not local to one file
Call the same route as an authorized caller to confirm it works, so a rejection is attributable to the guard rather than to a malformed request
Inspect the merge implementation itself rather than its name, since helpers with the same name differ in whether they skip prototype keys
Read the configured `query parser` setting before asserting an object-shaped query value is reachable, since the two parsers behave differently and the default differs by major version
Attempt the path escape through the framework's own file-serving API with `root` set, to confirm whether containment is already enforced
Confirm the deployment's `NODE_ENV` before treating default-handler stack output observed locally as something the caller would receive

root_causes: Enforcement depends on registration order, which is invisible at the call site and easy to break when a route module is imported earlier than expected
A second router or a second mount point is added without the guard the first one carries
Request fields are validated for value but not for type, so the parser's ability to produce objects and arrays is never considered
Objects are constructed by copying whatever the caller sent instead of by reading named fields
Recursive merges treat `__proto__` as an ordinary key because the merge helper was chosen for convenience rather than for its prototype handling
Limits are left at their defaults or raised globally to accommodate one large endpoint
Error detail is returned to help debugging and the environment variable that was supposed to suppress it is not set where it matters
Filesystem paths are assembled before they are constrained, so the check runs against a string rather than against the resolved location

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Make enforcement a property of the route rather than of the file's line order, and constrain every request value in shape as well as in content before anything is built from it
patterns: Attach the guard to the router the routes live on and construct that router in one place, so adding a route cannot silently opt out of it
Keep an explicit list of public routes and fail closed for anything not on it, rather than relying on a guard mounted early enough
Validate every request body, parameter, and query field against a schema that fixes the type and rejects unknown keys, before any handler logic reads it
Build objects by reading named fields rather than by copying the caller's object, so the property set is decided by the application
Use merge and clone helpers that skip prototype keys, or build into objects created with a null prototype
Set body-size and element-count limits at each parser mount, and keep the tight default rather than raising it globally for one endpoint
Return a fixed error shape with a correlation identifier and log the detail server-side, so response content does not depend on an environment variable
Serve files through the framework's own file-serving API with an explicit root, and where a path must be built by hand, resolve it first and assert containment as a whole path component
Set `trust proxy` to the specific number of hops or the specific proxy in front of the process, never to a blanket true

assertions: The vulnerable ownership fixture scopes the list path but re-fetches by primary key on the export path with no predicate, so one path enforces and its sibling does not — the framework-neutral form of a second router that never received the guard
The remediated ownership fixture resolves objects through a call that requires the effective subject on both paths, and both paths still return the owner's data
The vulnerable object-update fixture copies every key of the request body onto the persisted object, so a caller-chosen property is written even though a field list is present in the file

The compensated object-update fixture keeps the identical whole-body copy and is safe only because the class declares `__slots__`, so undeclared attributes raise instead of being set; the copy alone is not the finding
The vulnerable path fixture rejects traversal sequences before decoding and then decodes and joins, so an encoded sequence survives the check and escapes the base directory
The remediated path fixture decodes first, reduces to a basename, and asserts the resolved path is inside the base directory before writing, while still storing legitimately named files

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: The referenced fixtures are framework-neutral synthetic cases in another language; they exercise the invariants this pack anchors on, not the Express API surface itself
Middleware order is decided by module import order as well as by the lines in one file, so a conclusion drawn from a single file is provisional until the whole registration sequence is read

Behaviour differs between the 4.x and 5.x lines — notably the default `query parser` and the route pattern syntax — and an application can override the default in either, so the configured setting is the authority rather than the version
Third-party middleware decides much of the real behaviour, including body limits, upload handling, and rate limiting, and its configuration may live outside the reviewed repository
Prototype pollution consequences depend on which object the polluted prototype later reaches, which a single observation does not establish; the impact claim needs its own path
